blocks.html: Those who give themselves up as prey to the immodest love of women let themselves be so consumed and overcome, little by little, by this mad passion that they sometimes lose their senses by it; and being unable to make a breach in the honour of the woman they pursue, in order to satisfy the lasciviousness of their unbridled desires and disordered appetites, they use a thousand blandishments, wiles and deceptions, nay often have recourse to force — whence is contracted the crime which we call Rape [rapt: in the law of the time, abduction as well as rape], and of which our gallant du Tilh remains sufficiently attainted and convicted. This Rape had been committed upon a married woman, and was therefore undoubtedly worthy of death a. For a woman is ravished not only when she is violated and carried off from one place to another by force b, but also when she is seduced and suborned by ruses, cunning, baits and false persuasions c; and then the Rape is punished no less than if it had been committed and executed by force d: both because a will extorted by wiles, or by some fraud, does not warrant the trickster, nor cover his crime e; and also because to persuade craftily, with ruses and false and honeyed enticements, is no less than to force and constrain f. And so, in like terms, Ulpian the Jurisconsult answers that he who keeps a free person in his house, although it be with that person's consent, and he is content with it, if nevertheless such affection and contentment proceed from the cunning, subornation and false representations of him who keeps him, is no less culpable than if he kept him by force g. And thus are to be understood the texts of our laws which seem to require, for the crime of Rape, force and violence h. From this there follows a kind of excuse for the said de Rols: for a woman who has been forced cannot be charged with adultery, nor with any lechery i, even though for shame she has not at once declared it, and has expressly forbidden that it be told to her husband k; nay, the Emperor in these cases wills that the reputation of a woman of worth be inviolably and perpetually preserved to her l.

notes.citation: Digest 48.6 (Ad legem Iuliam de vi publica), l. Qui coetu, the last paragraph (D. 48.6.5.2, Marcian); Code 9.13 (De raptu virginum, seu viduarum, nec non sanctimonialium), the sole law (C. 9.13.1, Justinian)
notes.original: l. qui cœtu P. fi, D. de vi pub. l. vn. C. de rapt. virg.
notes.gloss: D. 48.6.5.2: he who carries off a woman, unmarried or married, is punished with the ultimate penalty — qui vacantem mulierem rapuit vel nuptam, ultimo supplicio punitur. C. 9.13.1 makes rape capital. The print's fi, is fin., the last paragraph; see the report on the `⟨alt⟩`.

notes.citation: Institutes 4.18 (De publicis iudiciis), § Item lex Iulia — two paragraphs of the title so begin (§§ 4, 8); the one on the lex Iulia de vi publica seu privata (Inst. 4.18.8), which makes rape capital, suits the point; Decretum, C. 36 q. 1, c. 2 Lex illa, with Gratian's dictum at its end, and c. 3 De raptoribus
notes.original: P. item lex Iulia. de pub. iud. c. lex. P. fi. c. de raptorib. xxxvj. q. i
notes.gloss: Causa 36 of the Decretum is the causa on raptus.

notes.citation: Code 9.13.1 (as at {a}); Authenticum, coll. 9, the Novel De raptu mulierum (Nov. 143 = Nov. 150, Ut raptae mulieres non nubant raptoribus), § 1; the Gloss on the rule Scienti in the Liber Sextus, De regulis iuris (VI, de reg. iur., reg. 27, Scienti et consentienti non fit iniuria neque dolus)
notes.original: l. vn. C. de rap. vir. P. j. de ra. mul. col. ix. Gloſe au c. ſcienti. de reg. iur. au vj.
notes.gloss: The rule says no wrong is done to one who knows and consents; the gloss is cited for its limit — consent procured by fraud is no consent.

notes.citation: Digest 47.10 (De iniuriis et famosis libellis), l. 1, § Usque adeo (D. 47.10.1.5, Ulpian); Code 1.7 (De apostatis), l. Eum (fragment not identified)
notes.original: l. P. vſque adeo. D. de in iur. l. eum. C. de apoſta.
notes.gloss: D. 47.10.1.5: the wrong done to our children touches our own honour, so that even if a son is sold with his consent the father has the action for iniuria in his own name — the wrong to the husband or father subsists though the woman was willing. The print's l. P. has lost the law's number (l. j.); the same text was cited at annot-046 {f} under a title there printed de in ius.

notes.citation: Code 9.13.1 (as at {a}), and Baldus (Balde) on it
notes.original: l vnique. & illec le Balde. C. de rap. vir.
l. j. P. perſuadere. D. de ſer. corrup.
notes.gloss: Persuadere autem est plus quam compellere atque cogere sibi parere — to persuade is more than to compel and force to obey; Coras's "no less than to force and constrain".

notes.citation: Digest 43.29 (De homine libero exhibendo), l. 3, § Si quis volentem (D. 43.29.3.5, Ulpian)
notes.original: l iij P. ſi. qs volentem. D. de lib. ho. exhib.
notes.gloss: The interdict against one who keeps a free man with evil intent: a willing person is not held with dolus — unless the willingness was procured by fraud. The margin's qs is the abbreviation of quis.

notes.citation: Institutes 4.18, § Item lex Iulia, and Decretum C. 36 q. 1, c. Lex and c. De raptoribus — the same places as at {b}
notes.original: P. item lex Iulia. de pub iud. c. lex. P. fi. c. de raptoribꝰ. xxxvj q. j.

notes.citation: Digest 48.5 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis coercendis), l. Si uxor, § Si quis plane (D. 48.5.14(13).7, Ulpian), and l. Vim passam (D. 48.5.40(39) pr., Papinian); Digest 3.1 (De postulando), l. 1, and its § Removet (D. 3.1.1.6, Ulpian)
notes.original: l. ſi vxor. P. ſi quis plane. l. vim paſſã. D. de adult. l. j. l remouet. D. de poſtul
notes.gloss: Papinian: a woman who has suffered violence has not offended against the lex Iulia de adulteriis. D. 3.1.1.6: one who has been violated by brigands or enemies is not to be marked with infamy (non debet notari). Coras cites Removet as a separate law; it is a paragraph of l. 1.

notes.citation: Digest 48.5.40(39) pr., l. Vim passam, cited above at {i}
Code 9.9 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis et de stupro), l. Foedissimam (C. 9.9.20, Diocletian and Maximian)
notes.gloss: The constitution distinguishes the most foul wickedness of women who prostitute themselves from the case of those taken by force, whose reputation is to suffer no injury — Coras's "the Emperor wills that the reputation of a woman of worth be preserved to her". The same law is cited at annot-082 {u}. The transcribers could not settle whether the print's double s is ſs or ſſ; the word is the same.
